data.title: async / await
data.subtitle: Promise syntax; await yields, resume as microtask

cards.meaning: Syntax over Promises. It does not add a second thread or a new settlement model. It makes async control flow read like synchronous code while still yielding to the event loop at each await. Prefer it when there is branching, multiple steps, or try/catch clarity; thin wrappers can stay as .then chains.

Always a Promise — even with a plain return, callers get a Promise. A plain return value is wrapped as fulfillment; throw rejects that Promise. Returning an existing Promise adopts/flattens it (same idea as Promise.resolve) — callers get the inner value, not Promise<Promise<T>>.
cards.example: async function ok() { return 1; } // fulfilled 1; async function wrap() { return Promise.resolve(2); } // fulfills 2

cards.front: Can a non-async function use await?
cards.meaning: No — only async functions (and modules with top-level await) may use await as a keyword pause point. Using await in a non-async function is a syntax error, except special contexts like some REPL/module top-level cases.

cards.front: Does await block the JavaScript thread?
cards.meaning: No — it pauses the current async function and returns control to the caller / event loop so other code can run. When the awaited Promise settles, the rest of the function is scheduled as a microtask and resumes. It looks synchronous in source, but it never blocks like a busy while loop.

cards.front: log a; f() async with await; log b — order?
cards.meaning: a, f1, b, f2. f() starts and runs sync until await (f1); await suspends f; f() has already returned a Promise to the caller; sync caller continues (b); after the stack clears, microtasks run and f resumes (f2). Same rule for extra awaits in f: each resume is a microtask, and those beat later setTimeout(0).
cards.example: log a; f(); log b → a, f1, b, f2

cards.meaning: Yes. await x wraps non-Promises roughly like Promise.resolve(x); you still get an async pause/resume (microtask), even for plain values.
cards.example: async f: log 1; await 0; log 2; f(); log 3 → 1, 3, 2

cards.meaning: Throws at the await expression inside the async function, which rejects the async function's Promise unless caught.
cards.example: async function f() { await Promise.reject(new Error('no')); } f().catch(e => console.log(e.message)); // 'no'

cards.meaning: Each await is a suspension point; the remainder becomes a continuation like .then. That's why native try/catch works across those steps. Observable model: Promise return + microtask resume.
cards.example: await fetch; await res.json(); return user ≈ fetch().then(res => res.json()).then(user => user)

cards.meaning: Rejections from awaited Promises and synchronous throws in the try body — one style for sync and async failures. Recover: catch return fallback. Fail outward: catch log + throw (rejects the async function's Promise). Cleanup always: finally. Caller handles: omit catch; let the async Promise reject.

cards.front: If the returned Promise rejects and nobody awaits it?
cards.meaning: Unhandled rejection still applies if nobody awaits or .catch-es it — same rule as Promises.

Accidental serialization when independent — second request starts only after first completes (~2× slower). If B does not need A's result, do not await A before starting B. Fix: Promise.all([fetchUser(), fetchSettings()]) or kick off both first, then await: const userP = fetchUser(); const settingsP = fetchSettings(); return { user: await userP, settings: await settingsP }.

Each fetchItem waits for the previous, so N independent requests take roughly N times longer. Parallel: await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchItem)). If you fear overload, use a concurrency-limited pool — not full serial by default. Serial await is correct when each step needs the previous result (cursor pagination, dependent IDs) or policy says one-at-a-time. for await...of is for async iterables (pulls one at a time); it does not parallelize and is not a drop-in for an array of Promises.
ES modules in supporting environments/bundlers. Module evaluation waits on that await; importers wait on the module graph. Not available in classic scripts / plain CJS without wrapping.

cards.front: Calling an async function without await/.then?
cards.meaning: The caller races ahead. The work is in flight; you didn't wait for it. Forgetting that async functions return Promises is the trap.
Swallows errors and can return undefined unintentionally. Catch should recover with a fallback, rethrow, or otherwise handle on purpose.

cards.front: Does sync heavy CPU after await still block?
cards.meaning: Yes. Once resumed, that JS still runs on the one thread. await yields; CPU after resume still blocks the thread. Independent awaits + Promise.all overlap host waiting, not parallel CPU.
